name: Grace Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Hartley Rural Supplies, which sells feed, fencing, seed and tools to farm shops across three counties. I'm in at half past seven with a flask of tea, and I go through the orders from the farm shops. Then I ring the mills and the fencing makers to keep the shelves full before lambing and planting. I know most of the suppliers by first name, and I like it when old Mr Ashby at the feed mill asks after my children.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Daniel is a mechanic at a tractor dealer. We have Ruth, who's ten, and Josiah, who's seven, and we're in a mortgage for a house near the church. We go to church most Sundays and my mother looks after the children after school. I'm 43 and I came into buying late, after years on the shop counter, so I'm still the new girl on the buying side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with it. At work I'd say a computer can't tell you which farmer pays late or which mill stands by its word. At church I'd say nothing, because there are better things to talk about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit uneasy, but it's the weather and the prices that worry me, not computers. A wet spring cuts what farmers buy, and when farmers spend less, Hartley cuts back on everything. We've got a mortgage and Daniel's wage depends on farms buying machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and keep my head down. I'd keep saving the little we can, about a hundred and fifty a month, and I'd say yes to extra work at lambing time when the order book is heaviest. I'd also keep going to church and the Tuesday coffee morning, because that's where you hear what's going on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like an ordinary Tuesday. A bit of weight, because money's never relaxed, but nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if the business had a bad season?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother, and the church. Last winter when Josiah was in hospital for a week, the ladies from church cooked for us, and my mother took Ruth. I wouldn't ask the government for a penny, but I'd ask my own people without thinking twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever use a computer tool beyond the order screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the stock system, and I don't like it. I prefer the phone and a paper order book. A man's voice tells you more than a screen, like when a mill owner says a delivery's coming and you can hear he doesn't believe it himself.

say: I'd say a computer can't tell **who pays late** or which mill stands by its word.
I'd stay quiet at church; there are better things to talk about.
think: My worry is the **weather and prices**, because wet springs cut what farmers buy.
Daniel's wage also depends on farms buying machines.
do: Keep going and save about **a hundred and fifty** a month.
Take extra work at lambing time.
Keep going to church and the Tuesday coffee morning.
feel: Like an ordinary Tuesday, with a bit of **weight** from money.
S0.quote: I wouldn't ask the government for a penny, but I'd ask my own people without thinking twice.
fieldNote: Her **community** and mother are her safety net, and she says so plainly and without embarrassment.
Dislikes screens and trusts voices on the phone over systems, which she sees as her real skill.

steps.text: Keep ringing the mills and fencing makers for Hartley
Save a hundred and fifty a month towards the mortgage
Lean on my mother and church friends when money is tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too far, and I'd ask what it's doing to young people learning a trade. At work I'd say a good buyer needs a good ear. At church I'd say we should help those who lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the day-to-day ordering goes to computers, and that's half my week. I don't use AI, don't care to, and I'm not young. If Hartley kept just two buyers, I'd be the one who goes, because I never learned the new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the way I do and I'd try to be useful to the farmers directly. I'd do more of the farm visits, because walking a yard is something a computer can't do. I'd cut the little extras, the weekly treat and the swimming lessons, and I'd ask Daniel to take on weekend jobs fixing small engines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels sad, mostly. I like the job and I like being good at it, and now it's like the ground is shifting under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day is the part you most want to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone calls with farm shop owners, where you know the family and how the year's been. They are what make Hartley different from a website. I'd be sorry to lose that. I'd also keep the farm visits, boots on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Hartley cut a job, who would they pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The newest or the least useful on a screen, which would be me. Mr Hartley is fair, but the sons are running the books now, and they like numbers. I'd rather he told me straight, then I could make my plans.

say: I'd say it's **gone too far**, and ask what it does to young people learning a trade.
I'd say a good buyer needs a good ear.
think: The daily ordering, about **half my week**, goes to computers, and I'm the one who never learned the systems.
If Hartley kept two buyers, I'd be the one to go.
do: Do more **farm visits**, because walking a yard is something a computer can't do.
Cut the weekly treat and swimming lessons.
Ask Daniel to take weekend jobs fixing small engines.
feel: **Sad**, mostly, as if the ground is shifting.
S1.quote: The phone calls with farm shop owners, where you know the family and how the year's been. They are what make Hartley different from a website.
fieldNote: Sees her **personal** relationships with customers as her value, not her screen skills or a certificate.
Says plainly she'd rather be told straight by the firm than be left to guess.

steps.text: Make more farm visits and phone calls to the shop owners
Cut the weekly treat and the kids' swimming lessons
Ask Daniel to fix small engines at weekends for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for ordinary people, and our leaders should have thought of that before. At work I'd say nothing, because it'd do no good. At church I'd ask for prayers for families who might lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm out inside two years. If the machine can do my thinking, nobody needs a woman who learned buying on the job and doesn't use a computer. I'm 43, with two small children, and I'd have no idea what to do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by cutting every cost, sell Daniel's old truck, and put six hundred a month away. I'd go to the church and ask if anyone knows who's hiring, and I'd ask my mother to have the children more. I'd look for something hands-on, like helping at the feed mill, because I know the mill and I know the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels frightening. I wake up at night and I pray, but I also count the money in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to your church about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot. I'd tell Ruth and Josiah that Mummy might be at home more, that we're careful with money, and that we trust God and each other. I'd tell them to work hard at school and learn to do things with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth and Josiah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say anything fancy. I'd say it's not what we planned, but we'll look after each other, as we always do. The community has been there for generations, and I'd lean on that.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for ordinary people and our leaders should have planned.
I'd ask the church to pray for families who might lose work.
think: I'm **out inside two years**, since a machine can do my thinking.
At 43 with two small children, I'd have no idea what to do next.
do: Cut every cost, sell Daniel's old truck and put away **six hundred** a month.
Ask people at church who is hiring.
Look for hands-on work at the feed mill.
feel: **Frightening**; I wake at night, pray and count the money.
S2.quote: I'm 43, with two small children, and I'd have no idea what to do next.
fieldNote: Fear is concrete: **two children**, a mortgage and no tech skills.
Faith and community are the main plan, with the mill as the practical one.

steps.text: Sell Daniel's old truck and cut every extra cost
Put six hundred a month into savings
Ask my mother and church friends to help with the children
Ask the feed mill about hands-on work I could do

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. At work I'd tell them we should train the young ones in trades. At church I'd say we should support families, and apprenticeships matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still worried but I'd feel a bit more able to cope. I'd have time to get the kids a little older, and to put some money by. But I'm still the one who doesn't use the new tools, so I'd expect to be let go before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe two hundred and fifty a month, and try to be the person who does the farm visits and the phone work. I'd ask the mill if they'd take me for a trade role, like stores or dispatch, which are hands-on and will take longer to change. And I'd encourage Daniel to take on bigger repair jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel like I'm waiting for weather. You can see the clouds, you can't stop them, but you can bring the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: does it feel any different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retrain if I had to, but not on a screen. Something like a stores or dispatch certificate, or a college course in farm office work, where it's mostly practical. I don't like being the oldest in the classroom, but I'd do it for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain, if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit different. I'd have time to speak to the Hartleys and see what they'd do. But I know myself, and I'd probably put off anything difficult until the last minute, which is a weakness I should fix.

say: I'd say five years is **something**, at least, and we should train young people in trades.
I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever.
think: I'd cope a bit better, but I still expect to be **let go** before 2031.
I'm the one who doesn't use the new tools.
do: Save about two hundred and fifty a month and do the **farm visits** and phone work.
Ask the mill about stores or dispatch roles.
Encourage Daniel to take bigger repair jobs.
feel: Like **waiting for weather**: you can't stop the clouds but you can bring the washing in.
S3.quote: I feel like I'm waiting for weather. You can see the clouds, you can't stop them, but you can bring the washing in.
fieldNote: Expects to lose the job anyway, but treats time as a chance to get **practical**.
Admits she puts off hard things until the last minute.

steps.text: Save two hundred and fifty a month
Ask the feed mill about stores or dispatch work
Take a practical dispatch or farm office course, not on screen
Encourage Daniel to take on bigger repair jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, provided people actually do. At work I'd say train young people with their hands as well as their heads. At church I'd say pray and be neighbourly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel almost fine. By 2036 I'm 53 and Ruth is 20 and Josiah 17, so the big worry is what's left for them. I'd probably have moved out of buying by then, maybe into something at the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, and I'd pay the mortgage down as fast as I could. I'd take a short course when the time is right, probably something in stores or admin, and steer Ruth and Josiah toward trades or caring. I'd also build up the community side, help the church, and keep up with neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, like a long road. Still a bit of worry, but not enough to keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change about how you see your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes it feel like somebody else's problem, which is dangerous. I know that. So I'd write down one thing each year, and I'd ask Daniel to remind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Ruth and Josiah to be doing by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children in good work with their hands or hearts, a plumber or a nurse or a mechanic like their father. Work that needs a person in the room. And I'd want them to have faith and good friends, which matter more than any job.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, provided people do something.
I'd say train young people with their hands as well as their heads.
think: I'd feel almost fine; the big worry is what's left for **Ruth and Josiah**.
I'd probably have moved out of buying by 2036.
do: Pay the **mortgage** down as fast as I can.
Take a short stores or admin course when the time is right.
Steer the children toward trades or caring work.
feel: Manageable, like a **long road**, with a little worry.
S4.quote: I'd want my children in good work with their hands or hearts, a plumber or a nurse or a mechanic like their father.
fieldNote: Her eye is on the **children's** future more than her own job in this world.
Notices the risk of treating ten years as someone else's problem, and plans to be reminded.

steps.text: Pay the mortgage down as fast as possible
Take a short stores or admin course when the time is right
Steer Ruth and Josiah toward trades or caring work
Keep helping at church and with neighbours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time for the children to grow, no time for me to learn anything, and the mortgage doesn't wait. What would help is work that pays for hands, apprenticeships for people my age as well as the young, and a family-friendly firm that keeps good people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'm proud of. I'm proud that I learned this trade on the job and that farmers trust me, certificate or not. I'd hate for that to count for nothing.

headlineQuote: I'm proud that I learned this trade on the job and that farmers trust me, certificate or not.
portrait: Grace, 43, is a **junior buyer** for Hartley Rural Supplies, with a mechanic husband, two children and a mortgage.
She never uses AI, trusts voices on the phone more than screens and expects to be cut early.
Her safety net is family and church, and she prefers work and apprenticeships to handouts.
She is uneasy in mild worlds and alarmed in the fast ones, always thinking of her children first.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, with no time for the children to grow or her to learn.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for people her age, hands-on work, and firms that keep good people on.
